channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee voted 6-3 to hold Bank Rate at 3.75% for a sixth consecutive meeting, with three members voting for 4%, and Governor Andrew Bailey warned that prolonged Middle East conflict may require tighter policy.
item.description:
The vote matched both the July meeting and the median forecast in a Reuters poll of economists, and it is the last decision before next month's Budget. Bailey's formulation was careful: higher global energy costs have had a limited effect so far on UK price and wage setting, but the longer the volatility persists the bigger the effect on inflation, and the more likely it is that Bank Rate will need to be raised to return inflation to the 2% target. The domestic picture the committee is reading is mixed — inflation up to 3.1% on an uptick the reporting attributes largely to energy costs linked to the war in Iran, set against a slightly growing economy, 5% unemployment, falling vacancies and slowing wage growth. The committee said policy is being set to bring inflation down to 2% sustainably as the economy adjusts to the energy shock. Separately, and unanimously, it voted to reduce to zero the stock of UK government bonds held for monetary policy purposes and financed by central bank reserves; the reporting gives no timetable for that.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The interest of this decision is not the rate, which did not move, but the direction of the risk attached to it. A central bank holding while three of nine members vote to raise, with the governor naming the condition under which rates would need to rise, has told the market what the next change is likely to be rather than when. The condition he named is duration, not level — it is the persistence of energy volatility rather than the height of energy prices that he says would force policy tighter. That is a different thing to watch. It also establishes the general shape of the year for industrial buyers: an energy shock is being transmitted into monetary policy, and the tightening it produces arrives with a lag and affects construction and durable-goods demand rather than the energy price itself. The unanimous vote on the gilt stock is the quieter item and the reporting gives too little to read much into it. The 5% unemployment rate is a UK figure and belongs to a different labour market from the German one. Points that may be worth considering include whether UK demand assumptions allow for rates staying at or above the current level into 2027, and which end-markets in the UK book are most rate-sensitive.

MarketScreener | MarketScreener | The Independent | Cnyes

item.title: US President Donald Trump threatened very heavy tariffs and said he could treat as a hostile act Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's proposal to make Canada the EU's first associate member, which Mark Carney has welcomed.
item.description:
Trump called the prospect of Canada integrating with the bloc laughable and said that if he thinks it is at all a hostile act he will impose very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things; he also made the judgement conditional on intent, saying that if their intentions are good there will be no problem and if they are bad heavy duties will follow. The responses came quickly. The European Commission said the proposal is not a hostile act, that it is not finalised, and that it would require approval from EU member states. French Minister for European Affairs Benjamin Haddad said on 17 September that Washington has no right to veto EU decisions. Carney welcomed the proposal, framing it as building resilience on both sides, reducing vulnerability to geopolitical and economic pressure and enhancing independent decision-making and sovereignty rather than creating a rival power bloc. Republican Senator Susan Collins warned Carney that closer EU ties could make a deal with Washington harder to reach. Two of the reports add a structural point: "associate member" is not currently a legal designation in EU law, and formal membership requires a European country.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The gap between the threat and the thing threatened is unusually wide here, and that is the most useful thing about it. What exists is a proposal with no legal category to sit in, no member state approval, and no text; what has been threatened in response is tariffs on a trading relationship that is real and current. A threat conditioned on the speaker's reading of intent is also not a policy that can be planned against, because there is no trigger to monitor. What can be planned against is the linkage this instance shows: an EU trade policy decision drawing a US tariff response aimed at goods unconnected to the decision. For a German exporter to the US the exposure is to that linkage rather than to the Canada file itself. It is worth noting that the Commission has already set October as a deadline for its China measures, so two trade tracks with US and Chinese counterparties are running in the same weeks. Points that may be worth considering include how much finished-goods value crosses the Atlantic on tariff schedules that a broad measure would reach, and whether pricing assumptions for the US market carry any allowance for a tariff change arriving without a specific trigger.

Politico Europe | Il Sole 24 Ore | Dunya Gazetesi | Commercial Times | CBC | The Economic Times

item.title: The German Chemical Industry Association welcomes some measures in Ursula von der Leyen's State of the European Union address but says Europe is too expensive as an industrial location in almost every respect.
item.description:
The association's response has three parts. It accepts that some of the announced measures point in the right direction. It says the need for action on location conditions in particular remains significant. And through chief executive Wolfgang Große Entrup it makes the cost argument in the broadest available terms: Europe as an industrial location is too expensive in almost every respect. The attribution of responsibility is the specific part — Brussels itself bears a significant share of the blame for regulatory costs, with new regulations constantly being added to the existing burdens. The statement carries no figure. It does not quantify the cost gap, name which of the announced measures the association welcomes, or specify which regulations it wants withdrawn.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

This is advocacy rather than measurement, and it is worth reading as such: an association's job at the moment a Commission president sets out a programme is to price the gap between what was announced and what its members need, and the currency it uses is emphasis rather than data. The content that survives that discount is the choice of target. Große Entrup's argument is not that energy is expensive, or that demand is weak, but that the cumulative stock of regulation is the cost — the complaint is about accretion, new rules landing on existing ones, rather than about any single rule. That is a harder thing for a Commission to answer than a specific file, because it implies subtraction rather than better design. The absence of a figure also limits what can be done with the statement operationally; it establishes a position, not a cost. Nothing in the reporting gives a European or German volume figure to set the cost argument against, so how much of the burden the association describes is being carried by weak volume cannot be read from this. Points that may be worth considering include which regulatory cost items in European operations are cumulative rather than one-off, and whether a simplification agenda that removes rules rather than adding better ones would change any current investment case.

VCI

item.title: US housing starts fell 2.6% in August to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.28 million units, with single-family starts up 7.6% to 918,000 and multifamily down 21.7% to 357,000; overall permits fell 2.7% to an annualised 1.39 million.
item.description:
The two halves of the headline move in opposite directions, and the permit data does not follow the starts data. On starts, the entire decline is multifamily: applying the reported rates to the reported levels, multifamily lost roughly 99,000 units of annualised pace while single-family added roughly 65,000, and the net is the 2.6% fall. On permits — the forward-looking series — both halves fell, single-family by 1.8% to an annualised 878,000 and multifamily by 4.3% to 516,000. So single-family starts rose in a month when single-family permits fell. Permits and starts are different series measured on different events, and the release does not give the inventory of units authorised but not started. The reporting is a National Association of Home Builders release carrying Census Bureau and HUD data; it does not give regional detail, completions, or the inventory of units authorised but not started.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Single-family and multifamily are not interchangeable from a materials standpoint, which is why the mix shift matters more here than the headline. A single-family unit carries considerably more construction adhesive, sealant and coating content than an apartment in a mid-rise does — more envelope area and more joint length per dwelling — so the mix shift offsets part of the unit decline. How much of it is not something the release settles: on these figures, single-family content per unit would have to be roughly one and a half times multifamily content per unit for total demand to be held flat, and no intensity figure is given. The permit data is the caution against extrapolating it: permits lead starts, and single-family permits fell in the same month single-family starts rose, which makes the rebound a monthly move rather than an established turn. The multifamily fall is the larger movement in absolute terms and it is concentrated in the segment most sensitive to financing conditions, which is where a reversal would come from if one came. Points that may be worth considering include whether US construction demand assumptions are keyed to unit counts or to the single-family share within them, and how quickly a mix shift of this kind shows up in channel orders.

NAHB

item.title: Billerud's Packaging Tomorrow 2026 report identifies six trends and finds companies increasingly seeking alternatives to fossil-based materials while reducing packaging weight and material use without compromising performance.
item.description:
The report is a materials producer's read on where packaging design is heading rather than a measurement of packaging demand, and the distinction is worth keeping. Four of its findings are reported. Sustainability is described as a key business priority; sustainability goals, regulation and consumer expectations are given as the three forces together driving companies away from fossil-based materials and towards less weight and less material. Circularity is moving from ambition to business requirement, with new regulations and recyclability requirements pushing companies to consider the entire packaging lifecycle from the design stage. The global paper packaging market is expected to grow faster than plastic; no rate is given for either. And 79% of US consumers are reported as more likely to buy products with QR codes, which the report ties to an expectation that content, origin and sustainability information arrives through the pack itself. The reporting names six trends but details only some of them, and gives no methodology, sample or date range for the consumer figure.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Lightweighting and recyclability pull in the same direction on material and in opposite directions on bonding, which is the tension a report like this tends to leave implicit. Less material in a pack means a thinner substrate, lower stiffness and less surface to bond to, so the joint carries more of the structural duty at the moment the material carrying it is being reduced. Design-stage lifecycle consideration, which the report describes as the new default, is also when adhesive and coating decisions are made, and it is the stage at which a debonding or recyclability requirement either gets specified in or does not. The paper-versus-plastic growth comparison has no rate attached, so it carries a direction rather than a magnitude; what it does suggest is a continued shift in substrate mix, and paper and plastic are not interchangeable from a bonding standpoint. The QR code finding is the one with the least direct bearing, though variable-data printing on a pack does place requirements on coating and surface. Points that may be worth considering include whether lightweighting targets reaching the business arrive as a performance specification or as a material specification, and how early in a customer's design cycle a recyclability requirement would have to be known to be met.

MarketScreener

item.title: The freight forwarders' association BGL has written an open letter to Chancellor Friedrich Merz asking for state relief, saying the net diesel price has risen by about EUR 0.60 a litre since the recent Middle East escalation.
item.description:
The association puts the cost through in units rather than in the abstract, which is what makes the letter useful. At a monthly mileage of 10,000 kilometres the increase adds about EUR 1,800 per truck, and for a fleet of 50 trucks that is over EUR 1 million a year. The arithmetic is internally consistent: EUR 1,800 a month across 50 vehicles for twelve months is about EUR 1.08 million, and EUR 1,800 at EUR 0.60 a litre implies roughly 3,000 litres a month, or about 30 litres per 100 kilometres, which is a normal figure for a heavy truck. The rise is stated as a net price; the reporting does not define the term. It does not give the starting price level, the date from which the EUR 0.60 is measured beyond "the recent escalation in the Middle East", or what form of relief the association is asking for.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

This is a cost already in the market rather than a forecast of one, and it lands on the medium-sized German transport sector the association speaks for. A EUR 1 million annual increase on a 50-truck operation is not absorbable at haulage margins, which means it moves: either into freight rates, or into capacity leaving the market, and the second raises rates as surely as the first. For a manufacturer the exposure is the same in either case and it is not confined to inbound raw material — outbound distribution of finished goods on pallets is diesel-priced in the same way. The letter is also a marker of political direction rather than only of cost. An industry association addressing the Chancellor directly, with a per-truck figure rather than a general complaint, is the kind of intervention designed to be costed by a ministry. Points that may be worth considering include whether current freight contracts carry a fuel escalator or leave the increase with the carrier until renewal, and what a sustained EUR 0.60 net increase does to landed cost on the routes that carry the most volume.

Handelsblatt

item.title: The American Chemistry Council expects global chemical production to grow just 0.5% this year and US chemical output volumes to rise 0.5%, with only 12 of the 20 key US chemistry-consuming industries expected to expand in 2026.
item.description:
The association attributes the weak global figure to disruptions to chemical production around the world; the reporting does not itemise them. The more useful part of the forecast is its composition. Growth is concentrated in sectors linked to data centres — semiconductors, computers and electrical equipment — plus aircraft, oil and gas, and pharmaceuticals. That leaves eight of the twenty US chemistry-consuming industries not expanding, and the reporting does not name them or say by how much they are expected to contract. Nor does it give a comparison with 2025, a regional breakdown behind the global number, or the association's definition of the twenty industries.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Two different things are being said at once and they are worth separating. The global 0.5% is a production growth rate for the world; the 12-of-20 is a count of US end-markets, not a share of demand, and the association gives the two figures on those different scopes. A count and a rate do not convert into one another — eight industries not expanding could represent a small or a large share of US chemical consumption depending which eight they are, and the reporting does not say. What the composition does establish is that the expansion on offer is narrow and sits in end-markets that are not the traditional volume consumers of adhesive technologies. Aircraft is a genuine bonding-intensive market but a small one by volume; semiconductors and electrical equipment consume speciality chemistry at high value and low tonnage. The absence of construction, automotive and general packaging from the growth list is the part that reads directly onto an adhesive technologies demand plan. Points that may be worth considering include whether 2026 volume assumptions were built on a broader recovery than a 0.5% global rate supports, and how much of the growth that is available sits in high-specification, low-tonnage applications rather than in volume.

Society of Chemical Industry

item.title: German industry's order backlog rose 10.9% in the year to July and, in price-adjusted terms, 1.5% on June, reaching an all-time high in manufacturing with a reach of nine months; the automotive backlog fell while other vehicle construction drove the gain.
item.description:
The Federal Statistical Office figures come with a composition that changes their reading. The nine-month reach is the highest since the series began in 2015. The increase was particularly supported by "other vehicle construction", which the reporting says includes aircraft, ships, trains and military vehicles, and government armament expenditure is described as likely to have played a role; many new orders have recently been received in the category and production times there are comparatively long. Mechanical engineering added a slight positive contribution. The automotive backlog fell. Two of the three reports add that leading institutes have raised their German forecasts on rising exports and government spending, with the Ifo Institute expecting growth of 1.4% for 2026 — a separate series from the backlog and not comparable with the percentages above. The reporting does not give the automotive decline, the size of the other-vehicle-construction contribution, or the backlog level in absolute terms.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

A record backlog with a nine-month reach describes work already sold, not work being won, and the longer the reach the more of the record is explained by production time rather than by demand. Other vehicle construction is a long-cycle category, and the reporting says its production times are comparatively long — an aircraft or a naval vessel sits in a backlog for years — so a category of that kind taking in a burst of orders raises the aggregate reach mechanically. That is the first thing to hold separate from a demand reading. The second is the automotive decline, which runs against the aggregate and is the movement that matters most for an adhesive technologies business, since automotive is a far larger consumer of bonded assembly by volume than shipbuilding or rail; its size is not reported. A headline record and a falling backlog in your largest end-market can be true together, and here they are. The defence-linked categories are genuinely bonding-intensive but on a different specification base, with qualification cycles and approval regimes that are not transferable from automotive work. Points that may be worth considering include whether German volume assumptions are being taken from the aggregate backlog or from the automotive component of it, and what a shift in the industrial mix towards long-cycle defence and aerospace would require in qualification terms.

Wirtschafts Woche | Handelsblatt | Süddeutsche Zeitung

item.title: Asepto's USD 126 million greenfield plant at Ain Sokhna in Egypt is expected to start commercial production by the end of calendar 2026, adding 12 billion aseptic packs a year and taking combined India and Egypt capacity to 24 billion.
item.description:
The plant is the mechanism for a stated change of model: Asepto is shifting from an India-led export model to multi-location global manufacturing, with the Egyptian site expected to become a key production hub for markets spanning Europe, Africa, the Gulf, CIS and the Americas. The site is 30 acres and sits close to the Suez Canal, which is the relevant fact about its location given how much of the served market lies on the other side of it. The doubling is the clearest number in the reporting — 12 billion packs added to take the India-and-Egypt total to 24 billion, implying an existing base of 12 billion — and it is a capacity figure rather than a volume or an order figure. The reporting does not give current utilisation, committed offtake, the product mix the Egyptian lines will run, or a ramp schedule beyond the end-2026 start.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Aseptic cartons are a multi-layer laminate — paperboard, polymer and aluminium foil bonded together — so an aseptic capacity addition is a laminating adhesive demand addition, and a doubling of one company's capacity is a large step in a market with few producers. The qualification point is the one that usually determines whether that demand is addressable: a new site running new lines settles its material set early, and this plant is already in customer trials with commercial production expected by the end of the year, so the window in which those choices are open is a short one. The geography is the second consideration. A plant positioned at the Suez Canal to serve Europe, Africa, the Gulf, CIS and the Americas is deliberately placed to be freight-competitive into several regions at once, which makes it a different kind of competitor to regional converters than an Indian export base was. Capacity is not volume, and nothing in the reporting says the 24 billion will be used; the figure describes what can be run, not what has been sold. Points that may be worth considering include whether laminating adhesive positions at new aseptic sites are being qualified during trials rather than after start-up, and what a second large low-cost aseptic base does to converter pricing in the regions it reaches.

The Economic Times

item.title: The Financial Times reports that the EU has asked China to limit hybrid car exports to 15% — of the EU market on one account, of the hybrid segment on another — and to limit exports of other products including chemicals.
item.description:
The 15% figure is reported on two different bases and the difference matters. The Association of European Vehicle Logistics carries it as about 15% of the EU market; La Vanguardia carries it as 15% of the segment, against over 33% today. Both attribute the story to the Financial Times, and neither the basis nor the reconciliation is given in the reporting. The chemicals element is stated in two of the three reports without a figure attached: China has also been asked to limit exports of other products, chemicals among them, while the EU separately seeks to increase Chinese purchases of European goods. La Vanguardia puts the trade imbalance the Commission is trying to correct at EUR 1 billion a day and October as the deadline for deploying measures. An EU official is quoted by Valor Econômico saying that if China does not limit its exports to the EU market, the EU will do so. The reporting does not say which chemical categories are in scope, what level is being proposed for them, or whether China has responded.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The headline is about cars and the sentence that matters to a chemical producer is the subordinate clause. A voluntary export restraint asked of a trading partner is a different instrument from a tariff: it is negotiated rather than imposed, it is quantity-based rather than price-based, and it does not need an anti-subsidy investigation behind it, which is why it can cover a list of products rather than a single one. That breadth is the point of interest here — an instrument built to be extended is easier to extend. The two bases for the 15% are not a detail either. Fifteen per cent of a segment where Chinese vehicles hold over a third implies a reduction of more than half; fifteen per cent of the whole EU market is a much weaker constraint, and the reporting does not settle which is meant. The official's remark that the EU will act if China does not is the clearest signal of direction, and it sets the October deadline as the date to watch rather than any figure. Points that may be worth considering include which imported chemical categories would be most exposed to a quantity restraint of this kind, and whether supply plans that assume Chinese intermediate availability have a European or other fallback qualified.

La Vanguardia | Association of European Vehicle Logistics | Valor Econômico

item.title: Oil fell about 1% on 18 September for a third consecutive session but stayed above USD 100, after Brent dropped 2.5% to USD 103.13 a barrel in intraday trade on 17 September as reported extra Saudi cargoes through Oman eased supply concern.
item.description:
The two price points are from different days and form a sequence rather than a single move. On 17 September Brent was down 2.5%, or USD 2.67, at USD 103.13 at 12:03 ET and West Texas Intermediate down 1.6% at USD 100.82, both one-week lows. On 18 September prices fell around 1% again, extending losses to a third session while holding above USD 100. Two developments are given for the easing, both at one remove. People familiar with the matter say Saudi Arabia is offering more crude cargoes to Asian refiners through ship-to-ship transfers off Oman's Sohar port; and an analyst quoted in the reporting attributes the retreat from weekly highs to US Energy Secretary Chris Wright signalling a quicker return to service for the East-West pipeline. The damage behind the disruption is now better described — three of the pipeline's pumping stations were damaged according to satellite imagery and three industry sources, and traders put a prolonged closure of the route to Yanbu at as much as 4% of global oil supply. Markets largely shrugged off fresh strikes exchanged between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthis. The reporting does not give a repair timetable, the volume moving through Oman, or the current Yanbu loading status beyond the earlier suspension.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Three sessions of decline with Brent still above USD 100 describes a market that has repriced the routing problem, not the supply problem. The two developments driving it are of different kinds and have different durability: ship-to-ship transfer off a port is a workaround that can be withdrawn as easily as it was offered, while a pipeline returning to service is a change in physical capability — but the second is a signal from a third-party official rather than an announcement from the operator, and three damaged pumping stations is a repair scope, not a date. The 4% of global supply figure is a traders' estimate of what a prolonged closure would remove; it is not on the same basis as the volume now moving via Oman, which is not given, and the two do not net against each other. For a buyer the practical content is that the floor has not moved: the easing has taken the panic premium out while leaving crude above USD 100, which is where the pass-through into petrochemical feedstock and energy-intensive intermediates is set. Points that may be worth considering include whether hedging and contract assumptions are anchored to the direction of the last three sessions or to the USD 100 level itself, and which European-delivered streams still depend on the Red Sea route.

The Hindu Business Line | Business Recorder | The Globe and Mail

item.title: Allnex is expanding sag control agent capacity at its Rayong site in Thailand, the company's first SCA manufacturing location outside Europe in more than 40 years, giving it access to automotive manufacturing centres across Asia.
item.description:
Sag control agents are rheology additives: they are what stops a wet coating running on a vertical surface before it cures, and they are a small-volume, high-specification input to automotive and industrial coatings. The reporting gives three reasons for the site choice — established infrastructure, technical expertise, and operational synergies with existing Allnex facilities — and three expected effects: stronger supply security, shorter lead times, and improved service for customers throughout APAC. The stated commercial logic is proximity to the automotive manufacturing centres of China, India, Korea and Southeast Asia. The reporting does not give the size of the expansion, the investment figure, a start date, or the current European capacity against which the Rayong addition should be read.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The detail carrying the most information is the forty years, because it dates the decision rather than describing it. A speciality additive made only in Europe for four decades is a product whose economics have tolerated a single-region supply base, and with it whatever freight and lead time serving other regions from Europe implies; moving it is a statement that something in that arrangement has stopped being tolerable. Which one is not said, and the three effects Allnex names — security, lead time, service — do not separate a response to customer pressure from a response to supply risk. The more general pattern is worth holding onto by anyone formulating in Europe for Asian end-markets: an additive supplier localising near the customer changes the qualification calculus for everyone downstream, because a locally made grade has to be re-qualified even when the specification is nominally identical. The absence of a capacity figure means the scale of the shift cannot be read from this. Points that may be worth considering include whether speciality inputs currently single-sourced from Europe would survive a lead-time test at Asian customer sites, and how long a re-qualification of a relocated additive grade typically takes in automotive coatings.

European Coatings
